title: Why can an octopus regrow an arm, but humans can't?
sentences: An octopus can regrow a lost arm, including its nerves and suckers, while you usually get a scar.
The difference is rebuilding, not just healing: its wound closes, then a growth region called a blastema helps reconstruct the arm.
Human wounds usually repair with scar tissue instead of rebuilding a whole limb.
But here's the twist: some human fingertip injuries can regenerate, especially when the nail region survives.
A fingertip is not an entire arm: rebuilding one needs coordinated bone, muscle, nerves and blood vessels.
Scientists are studying those signals, but no proven treatment regrows a lost human arm.
So search mammalian digit tip regeneration: what makes a fingertip rebuild while the rest of the limb cannot?

fact_check_notes: An octopus has arms, not tentacles; an arm is not an independent brain.
Do not claim octopuses never scar, all cells become embryonic stem cells, or a universal 100-day timeline.
Do not present deliberate evolutionary shutdown, cancer prevention or sepsis as a proven single explanation for human limb limits.
Fingertip regeneration depends on injury level and tissue context; it does not mean an entire finger or arm can regrow.
No claim that bioelectric stimulation is a proven human limb-regrowth treatment; imagery is illustrative, not evidence of a cure.
